articles.title: Logitech’s refurbished G Pro X2 Superstrike is 35 percent off
articles.description: The Superstrike looks similar to Logitech’s previous high-end gaming mice, but has haptics-based sensors instead of switches. | Image: Cameron Faulkner / The Verge Looking for a way to try the haptics-equipped G Pro X2 Superstrike wireless gaming mouse without spending full price? You probably aren’t alone. Logitech’s now-last-gen right-handed mouse is a great PC gaming companion that mimics the feel of mechanical switches with nothing but haptics. You can grab it refurbished through Logitech’s official eBay store for $131.74 (usually $179.99), and for even less with the code PROXPRODUCTS15 applied at checkout. It drops the price to just under $117. Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike Where to Buy: $179.99 $117 at eBay (refurb, w/ code PROXPRODUCTS15) The G Pro X2 Superstrike came out earlier this year, and I went hands-on with it. Logitech’s companion software lets you customize the intensity of the haptics, from an extra punchy click to one that’s barely there. (You can also turn the click feel off completely, but that felt a bit strange.) The mouse also supports rapid trigger, and when used together with haptics, it lowers the click latency compared with other mice that have mechanical switches. The company followed up recently with the X3 Superstrike, though its differences may not matter much to those who aren’t competitive gamers. The X3 features a more responsive sensor, better battery life, and improved weight distribution. There are some other somewhat small changes to the specs. That said, none of these improvements makes the X2 feel obsolete, and Logitech is continuing to support and sell the mouse. So, if you want to give it a try, now’s your chance to save quite a bit of money on the purchase. Read our hands-on of the X2 Superstrike.

articles.title: The Workforce Behind the Roadmap
articles.description: For three years, every semiconductor conference has featured some version of the same slide: the industry doesn’t have enough people to build what it’s promising. This month, SEMI’s National Network for Microelectronics Education (NNME), backed by the National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Commerce, named its first Industry Advisory Committee to turn those warnings into a national strategy, against a projected U.S. shortfall of 127,000 to 157,000 workers by 2030. The post The Workforce Behind the Roadmap appeared first on Semiconductor Digest.
